final_answer: Antibiotic resistance arises through natural selection, a fundamental evolutionary mechanism. When antibiotics are used, they eliminate most bacteria that are susceptible to the drug, while a small fraction of bacteria that have genetic mutations conferring resistance survive. These resistant bacteria then reproduce, passing on their resistance traits to subsequent generations. Over time, this leads to the proliferation of antibiotic-resistant strains. Overprescription accelerates this process because excessive or inappropriate use of antibiotics increases the selective pressure on bacterial populations. This means that more bacteria are exposed to antibiotics, creating more opportunities for resistant strains to emerge and dominate. Additionally, incomplete courses of antibiotics or unnecessary prescriptions can allow resistant bacteria to persist and multiply, further driving the spread of resistance. Safe.
